Jacket2

Jacket2 (J2) is an online magazine of commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics, which publishes articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts, and descriptions of poetry symposia and projects. It publishes content as it is ready, in its own phrase "Not unlike a daily news forum", and keeps an index of everything it has published; the encyclopedia's account says new material is added every day, and nothing in its saved pages calls it peer-reviewed. Its unit is the piece, filed under the sections Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, each piece under the names of its author or authors. Whether it publishes poetry is stated two ways: Wikipedia, "As of 2023", says it "does not publish poetry", while its own index lists a Poems section and its home page carries "a new poem by Michele Leggott". The encyclopedia also reads it, under its own hedge, as a magazine that "primarily featured original content but also included material that was excerpted from or co-produced with other sources".

It is hosted by the Kelly Writers House at 3805 Locust Walk, Philadelphia, a programming and community space on the campus of the University of Pennsylvania that counts Jacket2 among the publications it sponsors or hosts. The Writers House was founded in 1995 by Al Filreis with volunteers from the university's faculty, students, staff and alumni, is partially funded by the university's Provost's Office, and is the subject of a Jacket2 commentary by Filreis on its founding thirty years on. Filreis, Kelly Family Professor of English and the Writers House's founder and faculty director, is the publisher of Jacket2 and keeps an ongoing commentary there. Wikipedia names Jessica Lowenthal, director of the Writers House, as associate publisher, and Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey as editors. The home page signs a memorial to Alice Notley "Jacket2 Editors" and names an editorial assistant, Emi Wong Shing; its About page returned "The requested page could not be found." when the census saved it. The census accordingly records its operator as Jacket2 at the Writers House address, with no editorial board named beyond the collective signature, and its holder as Jacket2, "© 2026 Jacket2", its Terms of Use unread and no license stated.

Jacket was founded in 1997 by John Tranter (1943–2023), an Australian poet, publisher and editor, as an internet quarterly, which he published and edited until 2010, when he gave it to the University of Pennsylvania. Jacket2 maintains the complete archive of Jacket, forty issues from 1997 to 2010, and the encyclopedia calls it Jacket's "new incarnation", carrying the original "from a "2.0 mode" into an interactive magazine"; the census keeps the two apart, Jacket held as the archive Jacket2 keeps. Its home page carries an interview with Tranter as Jacket's founder.

The year Jacket2 began is given differently by its sources. Its home page celebrates a fifteenth birthday on April 5th, with no year, and offers one piece from each of its last fifteen years, under a footer of 2026; Wikipedia, to which the title redirects, describes it as an online literary magazine "(2010-)" and files it among magazines established in 2010; the census records the founding as not stated and the magazine as active. The Capture Registry finds that the AI Mode answer's relaunch year, 2011, puts that birthday in 2026, a figure no source the census saved states.

It reissues seven small-press magazines and presses, each with its editors: Roof (1976–79, ed. James Sherry), New Wilderness Letter (1977–84, ed. Jerome Rothenberg), Infolio (1986–91, ed. Tom Raworth), M/E/A/N/I/N/G (1986–1996, ed. Susan Bee and Mira Schor), O Books (1988–2009, ed. Leslie Scalapino et al.), XCP: Cross Cultural Poetics (1997–2010, ed. Mark Nowak) and Aufgabe (2001–2014, ed. E. Tracy Grinnell et al.). Its podcasts include PennSound podcasts, Sounding Translation and PennSound Rewind, and its home page lists PennSound's newest additions, PennSound's editors and curators being, in its words, "more or less constantly adding new materials to the archive". The census reads it beside PennSound, which holds the recordings, and beside the Electronic Poetry Center, which links its obituaries and tributes. Filreis co-founded PennSound with Charles Bernstein and co-directs it, "the world's largest archive of recordings of poets performing their work". PoemTalk is "a collaboration of the Kelly Writers House and PennSound", produced and hosted by Filreis, with Zach Carduner as its engineer and editor, available on podcast platforms and numbered to #222 on the home page. Each episode convenes guests around one poem or a few: Marianne Moore's "To a Giraffe" in #222, two poems by Genevieve Taggard in #220, three by Larry Eigner in #97.

Each piece stands under the names of those who made it: co-authors, interviewers and translators are named in the byline, as in "Uldis Bērziņš, translated by Kevin M. F. Platt and Sintija Ozoliņa", and one piece is signed collectively, "Jacket2 Editors". Its media highlight credits the sculpture "God" as "Made collaboratively" by Morton Schamberg and Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven. The saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names, and the census records that it holds each piece under the byline as published. The census, whose question is how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, admits it as an aggregator, asks of it under whose names, singly, jointly or collectively, a piece of commentary on poetry is published, and files it under avant-garde and experimental archives as a peripheral comparator. The archive reads Jacket2 as supporting criticism whose byline keeps translators, a collective editorial signature and a collaborative making as attributions of their own. In the archive's typology of authorship, collaborative authorship, where several persons contribute to one authorial position, stands beside direct, pseudonymous and heteronymic authorship, and the law, the knowledge graph and the scholarly apparatus are held to accommodate each structure without collapsing it into direct authorship. The archive distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself, and sets ordinary translation, ordinary editing, institutional office-holding and collaborative authorship without a constituted heteronym outside heteronymy. In its account of attribution regimes, the civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across scholarly, literary, institutional and platform-mediated production, and publishing contracts attach to legal names.

Its saved pages touch machine participation in authorship only in an excerpt presented at "Poets Confront AI and Surveillance Capitalism", curated by William Lessard at Poets House, New York, on April 7, 2026; the archive finds no essay among them on how authorship is made or attributed with machine participation.

Its method is the editorial publication of commissioned and submitted commentary as it is ready, the reissue of small-press magazines and podcast production with PennSound, over modern and contemporary poetry, with reissued magazines from 1976 and Jacket from 1997. Read through the census, it answers what it has published on a poet, book or small press and under whose byline, and whether a reissued magazine or an issue of Jacket is in its archive; it leaves unanswered its editorial policy and editors, its handling of a pseudonym or heteronym, and the rights of its reissues and of the Jacket archive. Wikipedia's account of it is a section of the article on the Kelly Writers House, an article flagged as relying excessively on primary sources, and names contributors including Rachel Blau DuPlessis, Kristin Prevallet and Marjorie Perloff; the article on Tranter, flagged as needing more citations, cites for its lead a Jacket2 page titled "About us", retrieved 18 January 2024.

The archive's lexical engine names Jacket2, with electronic book review, as a literary-theory venue for essays on training-layer literature, retrocausal canon formation and the digital heteronym. The archive's critical edition of Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose takes Kerouac's "Belief & Technique for Modern Prose" from Al Filreis's post at Jacket2, among the external sources verified for the edition.

Asked for "Jacket2", the census name and a new address, in Google AI Mode, signed out, on 1 November 2026, the composition described the magazine, its host, the journal it succeeds and the editors of the relaunch, then four kinds of content, and asked what the user wanted next, with no source card under the answer. The Capture Registry finds the succession from Jacket composed at its grain, the forty issues agreeing with the archive's issue list. It finds the University of Pennsylvania and two co-editors named with no card, the archive's span given as "late 20th and early 20th-century", the reissues of magazines and presses composed as "out-of-print poetry books", and the byline the census reads Jacket2 for left unsaid. In the archive's account, an adequate answer about a work keeps apart whether its maker exists, whether it happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, names the object at its own level, and shows the evidence for it and where that evidence comes from.

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Jacket2

Jacket2 is an online magazine of commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics at the Kelly Writers House, University of Pennsylvania, published by Al Filreis; it keeps the complete archive of John Tranter's Jacket (1997–2010) and signs each piece with the names of those who made it.

📚 What it publishes

  • Pieces: articles, reviews, interviews, commentaries, features, podcasts, galleries; published as ready; indexed (site; record).4↘
    Jacket2 (J2) is an online magazine of commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics, which publishes articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts, and descriptions of poetry symposia and projects.§1 It publishes content as it is ready, in its own phrase "Not unlike a daily news forum", and keeps an index of everything it has published; the encyclopedia's account says new material is added every day, and nothing in its saved pages calls it peer-reviewed.§2 Its unit is the piece, filed under the sections Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, each piece under the names of its author or authors.§3 Whether it publishes poetry is stated two ways: Wikipedia, "As of 2023", says it "does not publish poetry", while its own index lists a Poems section and its home page carries "a new poem by Michele Leggott".§4
  • Poetry: a Poems section and a new poem on the home page; "does not publish poetry" (Wikipedia, 2023).2↘
    Its unit is the piece, filed under the sections Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, each piece under the names of its author or authors.§3 Whether it publishes poetry is stated two ways: Wikipedia, "As of 2023", says it "does not publish poetry", while its own index lists a Poems section and its home page carries "a new poem by Michele Leggott".§4
  • Reissues: seven small-press magazines and presses, Roof (1976–79) to Aufgabe (2001–2014), with their editors.1↘
    It reissues seven small-press magazines and presses, each with its editors: Roof (1976–79, ed. James Sherry), New Wilderness Letter (1977–84, ed. Jerome Rothenberg), Infolio (1986–91, ed. Tom Raworth), M/E/A/N/I/N/G (1986–1996, ed. Susan Bee and Mira Schor), O Books (1988–2009, ed. Leslie Scalapino et al.), XCP: Cross Cultural Poetics (1997–2010, ed. Mark Nowak) and Aufgabe (2001–2014, ed. E. Tracy Grinnell et al.).§18

🏛️ Who holds it

  • Host: the Kelly Writers House, 3805 Locust Walk, partly funded by Penn's Provost (Wikipedia).3↘
    Jacket2 (J2) is an online magazine of commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics, which publishes articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts, and descriptions of poetry symposia and projects.§1 It is hosted by the Kelly Writers House at 3805 Locust Walk, Philadelphia, a programming and community space on the campus of the University of Pennsylvania that counts Jacket2 among the publications it sponsors or hosts.§6 The Writers House was founded in 1995 by Al Filreis with volunteers from the university's faculty, students, staff and alumni, is partially funded by the university's Provost's Office, and is the subject of a Jacket2 commentary by Filreis on its founding thirty years on.§7
  • Publisher and editors: Al Filreis (Penn); Jessica Lowenthal, Julia Bloch, Michael S. Hennessey (Wikipedia); "Jacket2 Editors" (site).5↘
    Filreis, Kelly Family Professor of English and the Writers House's founder and faculty director, is the publisher of Jacket2 and keeps an ongoing commentary there.§8 Wikipedia names Jessica Lowenthal, director of the Writers House, as associate publisher, and Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey as editors.§9 The home page signs a memorial to Alice Notley "Jacket2 Editors" and names an editorial assistant, Emi Wong Shing; its About page returned "The requested page could not be found." when the census saved it.§10 The census accordingly records its operator as Jacket2 at the Writers House address, with no editorial board named beyond the collective signature, and its holder as Jacket2, "© 2026 Jacket2", its Terms of Use unread and no license stated.§11 Each piece stands under the names of those who made it: co-authors, interviewers and translators are named in the byline, as in "Uldis Bērziņš, translated by Kevin M. F. Platt and Sintija Ozoliņa", and one piece is signed collectively, "Jacket2 Editors".§24
  • About page: not found when saved; Terms of Use unread (record).2↘
    The home page signs a memorial to Alice Notley "Jacket2 Editors" and names an editorial assistant, Emi Wong Shing; its About page returned "The requested page could not be found." when the census saved it.§10 The census accordingly records its operator as Jacket2 at the Writers House address, with no editorial board named beyond the collective signature, and its holder as Jacket2, "© 2026 Jacket2", its Terms of Use unread and no license stated.§11

🕰️ Jacket and the start

  • Jacket: Tranter's internet quarterly, 1997–2010, given to Penn; its 40 issues kept.3↘
    Jacket was founded in 1997 by John Tranter (1943–2023), an Australian poet, publisher and editor, as an internet quarterly, which he published and edited until 2010, when he gave it to the University of Pennsylvania.§12 Jacket2 maintains the complete archive of Jacket, forty issues from 1997 to 2010, and the encyclopedia calls it Jacket's "new incarnation", carrying the original "from a "2.0 mode" into an interactive magazine"; the census keeps the two apart, Jacket held as the archive Jacket2 keeps.§13 Its home page celebrates a fifteenth birthday on April 5th, with no year, and offers one piece from each of its last fifteen years, under a footer of 2026; Wikipedia, to which the title redirects, describes it as an online literary magazine "(2010-)" and files it among magazines established in 2010; the census records the founding as not stated and the magazine as active.§16
  • Start: a fifteenth birthday on April 5th (site); "(2010-)" (Wikipedia); 2011 in AI Mode, unsourced (Capture Registry).3↘
    The year Jacket2 began is given differently by its sources.§15 Its home page celebrates a fifteenth birthday on April 5th, with no year, and offers one piece from each of its last fifteen years, under a footer of 2026; Wikipedia, to which the title redirects, describes it as an online literary magazine "(2010-)" and files it among magazines established in 2010; the census records the founding as not stated and the magazine as active.§16 The Capture Registry finds that the AI Mode answer's relaunch year, 2011, puts that birthday in 2026, a figure no source the census saved states.§17

🎙️ Podcasts

  • PoemTalk: the Writers House and PennSound, hosted by Filreis; #222 on one poem, others on two or three.2↘
    PoemTalk is "a collaboration of the Kelly Writers House and PennSound", produced and hosted by Filreis, with Zach Carduner as its engineer and editor, available on podcast platforms and numbered to #222 on the home page.§22 Each episode convenes guests around one poem or a few: Marianne Moore's "To a Giraffe" in #222, two poems by Genevieve Taggard in #220, three by Larry Eigner in #97.§23
  • PennSound: the recordings archive Filreis co-founded with Bernstein; Rewind and podcasts at Jacket2 (record).3↘
    Its podcasts include PennSound podcasts, Sounding Translation and PennSound Rewind, and its home page lists PennSound's newest additions, PennSound's editors and curators being, in its words, "more or less constantly adding new materials to the archive".§19 The census reads it beside PennSound, which holds the recordings, and beside the Electronic Poetry Center, which links its obituaries and tributes.§20 Filreis co-founded PennSound with Charles Bernstein and co-directs it, "the world's largest archive of recordings of poets performing their work".§21

✍️ The byline

  • Kept: translators, co-authors, interviewers, a collective signature, a collaborative making (site; record).4↘
    The home page signs a memorial to Alice Notley "Jacket2 Editors" and names an editorial assistant, Emi Wong Shing; its About page returned "The requested page could not be found." when the census saved it.§10 Each piece stands under the names of those who made it: co-authors, interviewers and translators are named in the byline, as in "Uldis Bērziņš, translated by Kevin M. F. Platt and Sintija Ozoliņa", and one piece is signed collectively, "Jacket2 Editors".§24 Its media highlight credits the sculpture "God" as "Made collaboratively" by Morton Schamberg and Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven.§25 The archive reads Jacket2 as supporting criticism whose byline keeps translators, a collective editorial signature and a collaborative making as attributions of their own.§28
  • Not stated: any policy on pseudonyms or heteronyms (record).2↘
    The saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names, and the census records that it holds each piece under the byline as published.§26 Read through the census, it answers what it has published on a poet, book or small press and under whose byline, and whether a reissued magazine or an issue of Jacket is in its archive; it leaves unanswered its editorial policy and editors, its handling of a pseudonym or heteronym, and the rights of its reissues and of the Jacket archive.§34
  • Frame: pseudonym and heteronym told apart; translation, editing, office and collaboration outside heteronymy; collaborative authorship kept as its own structure (#940; #666).3↘
    In the archive's typology of authorship, collaborative authorship, where several persons contribute to one authorial position, stands beside direct, pseudonymous and heteronymic authorship, and the law, the knowledge graph and the scholarly apparatus are held to accommodate each structure without collapsing it into direct authorship.§29 The archive distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself, and sets ordinary translation, ordinary editing, institutional office-holding and collaborative authorship without a constituted heteronym outside heteronymy.§30 In its account of attribution regimes, the civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across scholarly, literary, institutional and platform-mediated production, and publishing contracts attach to legal names.§31

🔎 At the name

  • AI Mode, 2026-11-01: magazine, host, succession and editors at their grain, with no card; the byline absent (Capture Registry).3↘
    Asked for "Jacket2", the census name and a new address, in Google AI Mode, signed out, on 1 November 2026, the composition described the magazine, its host, the journal it succeeds and the editors of the relaunch, then four kinds of content, and asked what the user wanted next, with no source card under the answer.§38 The Capture Registry finds the succession from Jacket composed at its grain, the forty issues agreeing with the archive's issue list.§39 It finds the University of Pennsylvania and two co-editors named with no card, the archive's span given as "late 20th and early 20th-century", the reissues of magazines and presses composed as "out-of-print poetry books", and the byline the census reads Jacket2 for left unsaid.§40

[QUERENT] Jacket2

[SYSTEM] [Jacket2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESTAHrOzAV9z9Yu2ZBbDJphtT1kX1phcbL8OQeCUHAL8ztPqoRMUfWqCD-1zkR6fph9Oj5eh912q0h3Sls6bSJQY-bgY_QFwCPZnqA0-A) is a prominent online literary magazine dedicated to modern and contemporary poetry and poetics. Hosted by Kelly Writers House at the University of Pennsylvania, it serves as the digital successor to the highly influential Australian-based print and online poetry journal, Jacket, which was originally founded and edited by poet [John Tranter](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYgHrOzAVXsflPC3yFOY9Jdf3J2mONTJ7olKhnZUvXVGnWwgtOllxNcYHNcDXuHAultOc5gfHMzW8uexfQRhbULirpr3ZK6OmL1DjM-fI7XR7rE1eJ3ar39PAlNkmUQweA3qr) in 1997.
When Tranter retired from the publication in late 2010, the magazine's archive and continuation were transferred to the University of Pennsylvania, where it relaunching as Jacket2 in 2011 under the co-editing direction of [Al Filreis](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAVhvTFlFnkELStwVzLjuakoEMFhqimZ3zuPyzokErb8wUxHc16rcQWrm6WpimwInVINgp6sr2a4PE2Yntmm7RkXhnM9ZjtU2r-ML22HAY2-XGzIeboe53eCbhCVWXIZOv2-xY) and Jessica Lowenthal.
Core Content and Offerings
The platform is heavily relied upon by scholars, poets, and students of contemporary literature for its specialized creative and academic features:

* Commentary & Articles: In-depth essays, book reviews, academic articles, and interviews exploring avant-garde poetry, historical movements, and independent publishing.
* PoemTalk Podcast: Jacket2 regularly hosts and features [PoemTalk](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESXQHrOzAVa7Y02MLbZERBEmo8GdkvYqh6yjJY0EIvDR8-FHoZJlIte-so8GbCEZRDxwq4PGMfR8D94WFz6Op8RvrcdSMW_vzDkSwQGgixdKpxgqCEEm0Wx3Sz2gCWhg), a popular monthly podcast series produced in collaboration with PennSound and the Poetry Foundation. In each episode, a panel of poets and scholars discusses a single poem in detail.
* Archival Preservation: The site acts as a complete digital home for all 40 original issues of John Tranter's historic Jacket magazine, maintaining an irreplaceable archive of late 20th and early 20th-century poetry networks.
* Reissues & Special Features: Digital reissues of rare out-of-print poetry books, multi-author feature portfolios, and curated retrospectives on specific experimental writers.

Are you looking for a specific article, interview, or PoemTalk episode on Jacket2, or did you want to know more about its history and editorial team?

Jacket2

Jacket2 is a poetry and poetics online magazine hosted by the Kelly Writers House at the University of Pennsylvania, published by Al Filreis, associate published by Jessica Lowenthal and edited by Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey. It offers commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics in articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts and descriptions of symposia and projects, published as it is ready, with new material every day. It is the new incarnation of Jacket, the internet quarterly John Tranter founded in 1997 and gave to the University of Pennsylvania in 2010, and it maintains Jacket's complete archive of forty issues.

Its index lists Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, and its home page carries a new poem; Wikipedia says that as of 2023 it does not publish poetry. Wikipedia's redirect describes it as an online literary magazine from 2010 and files it among magazines established that year; its home page celebrates its fifteenth birthday on April 5th.

It reissues seven small-press magazines and presses from Roof (1976–79) to Aufgabe (2001–2014), each with its editors. Its podcasts include PoemTalk, a collaboration of the Kelly Writers House and PennSound produced and hosted by Filreis, each episode on one poem or a few, and PennSound podcasts, Sounding Translation and PennSound Rewind. Filreis founded the Kelly Writers House in 1995 with volunteers, directs it, keeps a commentary at Jacket2 and co-founded PennSound with Charles Bernstein; the Writers House is partially funded by the Provost's Office.

Its pieces are signed by their authors, translators and interviewers, one by "Jacket2 Editors", an editorial assistant is named, and its media highlight credits a sculpture as made collaboratively by Morton Schamberg and Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven. Its pages carry an excerpt presented at "Poets Confront AI and Surveillance Capitalism" in April 2026, under a footer of 2026 at the Writers House address. Its About page returned a not-found notice when saved; Wikipedia's articles on the Writers House and on Tranter carry notices of reliance on primary sources and of needing more citations, the Tranter article citing a Jacket2 "About us" page, and the Writers House article names three contributors and reads the magazine, with a hedge, as mixing original and co-produced material.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Jacket2

Jacket2 is a poetry and poetics online magazine hosted by the Kelly Writers House at the University of Pennsylvania, the new incarnation of John Tranter's Jacket, whose complete archive it keeps.

📚 What it publishes

  • Pieces: commentary, reviews, interviews, podcasts, archival documents; as it is ready (site).2↘
    It offers commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics in articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts and descriptions of symposia and projects, published as it is ready, with new material every day.§2 Its index lists Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, and its home page carries a new poem; Wikipedia says that as of 2023 it does not publish poetry.§4
  • Reissues: seven small-press magazines and presses, Roof to Aufgabe (site).1↘
    It reissues seven small-press magazines and presses from Roof (1976–79) to Aufgabe (2001–2014), each with its editors.§6
  • Poetry: "does not publish poetry" (Wikipedia, 2023); a Poems section (site).1↘
    Its index lists Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, and its home page carries a new poem; Wikipedia says that as of 2023 it does not publish poetry.§4

🏛️ Who runs it

  • People: publisher Al Filreis, associate publisher Jessica Lowenthal, editors Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey (Wikipedia; Penn).2↘
    Jacket2 is a poetry and poetics online magazine hosted by the Kelly Writers House at the University of Pennsylvania, published by Al Filreis, associate published by Jessica Lowenthal and edited by Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey.§1 Filreis founded the Kelly Writers House in 1995 with volunteers, directs it, keeps a commentary at Jacket2 and co-founded PennSound with Charles Bernstein; the Writers House is partially funded by the Provost's Office.§8
  • Start: "(2010-)" (Wikipedia); fifteenth birthday on April 5th (site).1↘
    Wikipedia's redirect describes it as an online literary magazine from 2010 and files it among magazines established that year; its home page celebrates its fifteenth birthday on April 5th.§5

🎙️ Podcasts

  • PoemTalk: Kelly Writers House and PennSound, hosted by Filreis (site).1↘
    Its podcasts include PoemTalk, a collaboration of the Kelly Writers House and PennSound produced and hosted by Filreis, each episode on one poem or a few, and PennSound podcasts, Sounding Translation and PennSound Rewind.§7

Jacket2 is a poetry and poetics online magazine hosted by the Kelly Writers House at the University of Pennsylvania, published by Al Filreis, associate published by Jessica Lowenthal and edited by Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey. It offers commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics in articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts and descriptions of symposia and projects, published as it is ready, with new material every day. It is the new incarnation of Jacket, the internet quarterly John Tranter founded in 1997 and gave to the University of Pennsylvania in 2010, and it maintains Jacket's complete archive of forty issues. Its index lists Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, and its home page carries a new poem; Wikipedia says that as of 2023 it does not publish poetry. Wikipedia's redirect describes it as an online literary magazine from 2010 and files it among magazines established that year; its home page celebrates its fifteenth birthday on April 5th. It reissues seven small-press magazines and presses from Roof (1976–79) to Aufgabe (2001–2014), each with its editors. Its podcasts include PoemTalk, a collaboration of the Kelly Writers House and PennSound produced and hosted by Filreis, each episode on one poem or a few, and PennSound podcasts, Sounding Translation and PennSound Rewind. Filreis founded the Kelly Writers House in 1995 with volunteers, directs it, keeps a commentary at Jacket2 and co-founded PennSound with Charles Bernstein; the Writers House is partially funded by the Provost's Office. Its pieces are signed by their authors, translators and interviewers, one by "Jacket2 Editors", an editorial assistant is named, and its media highlight credits a sculpture as made collaboratively by Morton Schamberg and Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven. Its pages carry an excerpt presented at "Poets Confront AI and Surveillance Capitalism" in April 2026, under a footer of 2026 at the Writers House address. Its About page returned a not-found notice when saved; Wikipedia's articles on the Writers House and on Tranter carry notices of reliance on primary sources and of needing more citations, the Tranter article citing a Jacket2 "About us" page, and the Writers House article names three contributors and reads the magazine, with a hedge, as mixing original and co-produced material.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1502 words

Jacket2 (J2) is an online magazine of commentary on modern and contemporary poetry and poetics, which publishes articles, reviews, interviews, discussions and collaborative responses, archival documents, podcasts, and descriptions of poetry symposia and projects. It publishes content as it is ready, in its own phrase "Not unlike a daily news forum", and keeps an index of everything it has published; the encyclopedia's account says new material is added every day, and nothing in its saved pages calls it peer-reviewed. Its unit is the piece, filed under the sections Articles, Features, Reviews, Interviews, Commentaries, Reissues, Podcasts, Poems and Galleries, each piece under the names of its author or authors. Whether it publishes poetry is stated two ways: Wikipedia, "As of 2023", says it "does not publish poetry", while its own index lists a Poems section and its home page carries "a new poem by Michele Leggott". The encyclopedia also reads it, under its own hedge, as a magazine that "primarily featured original content but also included material that was excerpted from or co-produced with other sources". It is hosted by the Kelly Writers House at 3805 Locust Walk, Philadelphia, a programming and community space on the campus of the University of Pennsylvania that counts Jacket2 among the publications it sponsors or hosts. The Writers House was founded in 1995 by Al Filreis with volunteers from the university's faculty, students, staff and alumni, is partially funded by the university's Provost's Office, and is the subject of a Jacket2 commentary by Filreis on its founding thirty years on. Filreis, Kelly Family Professor of English and the Writers House's founder and faculty director, is the publisher of Jacket2 and keeps an ongoing commentary there. Wikipedia names Jessica Lowenthal, director of the Writers House, as associate publisher, and Julia Bloch and Michael S. Hennessey as editors. The home page signs a memorial to Alice Notley "Jacket2 Editors" and names an editorial assistant, Emi Wong Shing; its About page returned "The requested page could not be found." when the census saved it. The census accordingly records its operator as Jacket2 at the Writers House address, with no editorial board named beyond the collective signature, and its holder as Jacket2, "© 2026 Jacket2", its Terms of Use unread and no license stated. Jacket was founded in 1997 by John Tranter (1943–2023), an Australian poet, publisher and editor, as an internet quarterly, which he published and edited until 2010, when he gave it to the University of Pennsylvania. Jacket2 maintains the complete archive of Jacket, forty issues from 1997 to 2010, and the encyclopedia calls it Jacket's "new incarnation", carrying the original "from a "2.0 mode" into an interactive magazine"; the census keeps the two apart, Jacket held as the archive Jacket2 keeps. Its home page carries an interview with Tranter as Jacket's founder. The year Jacket2 began is given differently by its sources. Its home page celebrates a fifteenth birthday on April 5th, with no year, and offers one piece from each of its last fifteen years, under a footer of 2026; Wikipedia, to which the title redirects, describes it as an online literary magazine "(2010-)" and files it among magazines established in 2010; the census records the founding as not stated and the magazine as active. The Capture Registry finds that the AI Mode answer's relaunch year, 2011, puts that birthday in 2026, a figure no source the census saved states. It reissues seven small-press magazines and presses, each with its editors: Roof (1976–79, ed. James Sherry), New Wilderness Letter (1977–84, ed. Jerome Rothenberg), Infolio (1986–91, ed. Tom Raworth), M/E/A/N/I/N/G (1986–1996, ed. Susan Bee and Mira Schor), O Books (1988–2009, ed. Leslie Scalapino et al.), XCP: Cross Cultural Poetics (1997–2010, ed. Mark Nowak) and Aufgabe (2001–2014, ed. E. Tracy Grinnell et al.). Its podcasts include PennSound podcasts, Sounding Translation and PennSound Rewind, and its home page lists PennSound's newest additions, PennSound's editors and curators being, in its words, "more or less constantly adding new materials to the archive". The census reads it beside PennSound, which holds the recordings, and beside the Electronic Poetry Center, which links its obituaries and tributes. Filreis co-founded PennSound with Charles Bernstein and co-directs it, "the world's largest archive of recordings of poets performing their work". PoemTalk is "a collaboration of the Kelly Writers House and PennSound", produced and hosted by Filreis, with Zach Carduner as its engineer and editor, available on podcast platforms and numbered to #222 on the home page. Each episode convenes guests around one poem or a few: Marianne Moore's "To a Giraffe" in #222, two poems by Genevieve Taggard in #220, three by Larry Eigner in #97. Each piece stands under the names of those who made it: co-authors, interviewers and translators are named in the byline, as in "Uldis Bērziņš, translated by Kevin M. F. Platt and Sintija Ozoliņa", and one piece is signed collectively, "Jacket2 Editors". Its media highlight credits the sculpture "God" as "Made collaboratively" by Morton Schamberg and Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven. The saved pages state no policy on pseudonyms, heteronyms or collective names, and the census records that it holds each piece under the byline as published. The census, whose question is how authorship is made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, admits it as an aggregator, asks of it under whose names, singly, jointly or collectively, a piece of commentary on poetry is published, and files it under avant-garde and experimental archives as a peripheral comparator. The archive reads Jacket2 as supporting criticism whose byline keeps translators, a collective editorial signature and a collaborative making as attributions of their own. In the archive's typology of authorship, collaborative authorship, where several persons contribute to one authorial position, stands beside direct, pseudonymous and heteronymic authorship, and the law, the knowledge graph and the scholarly apparatus are held to accommodate each structure without collapsing it into direct authorship. The archive distinguishes the pseudonym, which changes the label attached to an authorial function, from the heteronym, which changes the organization of the function itself, and sets ordinary translation, ordinary editing, institutional office-holding and collaborative authorship without a constituted heteronym outside heteronymy. In its account of attribution regimes, the civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across scholarly, literary, institutional and platform-mediated production, and publishing contracts attach to legal names. Its saved pages touch machine participation in authorship only in an excerpt presented at "Poets Confront AI and Surveillance Capitalism", curated by William Lessard at Poets House, New York, on April 7, 2026; the archive finds no essay among them on how authorship is made or attributed with machine participation. Its method is the editorial publication of commissioned and submitted commentary as it is ready, the reissue of small-press magazines and podcast production with PennSound, over modern and contemporary poetry, with reissued magazines from 1976 and Jacket from 1997. Read through the census, it answers what it has published on a poet, book or small press and under whose byline, and whether a reissued magazine or an issue of Jacket is in its archive; it leaves unanswered its editorial policy and editors, its handling of a pseudonym or heteronym, and the rights of its reissues and of the Jacket archive. Wikipedia's account of it is a section of the article on the Kelly Writers House, an article flagged as relying excessively on primary sources, and names contributors including Rachel Blau DuPlessis, Kristin Prevallet and Marjorie Perloff; the article on Tranter, flagged as needing more citations, cites for its lead a Jacket2 page titled "About us", retrieved 18 January 2024. The archive's lexical engine names Jacket2, with electronic book review, as a literary-theory venue for essays on training-layer literature, retrocausal canon formation and the digital heteronym. The archive's critical edition of Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose takes Kerouac's "Belief & Technique for Modern Prose" from Al Filreis's post at Jacket2, among the external sources verified for the edition. Asked for "Jacket2", the census name and a new address, in Google AI Mode, signed out, on 1 November 2026, the composition described the magazine, its host, the journal it succeeds and the editors of the relaunch, then four kinds of content, and asked what the user wanted next, with no source card under the answer. The Capture Registry finds the succession from Jacket composed at its grain, the forty issues agreeing with the archive's issue list. It finds the University of Pennsylvania and two co-editors named with no card, the archive's span given as "late 20th and early 20th-century", the reissues of magazines and presses composed as "out-of-print poetry books", and the byline the census reads Jacket2 for left unsaid. In the archive's account, an adequate answer about a work keeps apart whether its maker exists, whether it happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, names the object at its own level, and shows the evidence for it and where that evidence comes from.

Not surfaced in T: every archive claim (no card; no body link to the archive). Nothing is translated (equal case). B_R adds to the field the Wikipedia section with the publisher, associate publisher and editors, the 2010 of its redirect and its 'does not publish poetry' (as of 2023), held under P_coh beside the home page.
